links.outcome: Severity classification accuracy before vs after RAG grounding on retrieval and unseen test sets
links.effect: RAG improved accuracy on retrieval set (V3.2-B 56% to 70%, P=.002; V3.2-R 83% to 99%, P<.001) but not on unseen test set (V3.2-B 57% vs 59%, P=.61; V3.2-R 86% vs 81%, P=.33).
links.quote: Crucially, the performance gains observed in the retrieval set did not translate to the external test set, revealing a critical limitation in the generalizability of RAG for this specific task.

links.outcome: Comparing fast base LLM with reasoning LLM for subjective severity grading
links.effect: Base model 56.6% accuracy versus reasoning model 84.6%; base model recall 0 for minor anomalies.
links.quote: V3.2-B’s accuracy was only 56.7% (144/254), while V3.2-R significantly improved to 84.6% (215/254), with a macro- F 1 -score of 0.75.

links.outcome: LLM severity grading errors, missing serious/lethal anomalies
links.effect: Lethal malformation recall 0.40 with V3.2-R; base model missed all minor anomalies; overall severity accuracy 84.6%.
links.quote: it achieved perfect precision for “lethal malformation” but with low recall (0.40), while for “major malformation,” it achieved perfect recall at the cost of lower precision (0.53).

links.quote: These data indicate that while RAG can effectively guide LLMs to memorize or retrieve specific patterns within the knowledge base, it fails to significantly enhance—and may potentially hinder—performance on unseen, heterogeneous clinical data.
